facts.value: Employers examine job applicants' public social media profiles as part of the hiring assessment.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: The vast majority of Fortune 500 companies use social media as a tool to screen prospective employees and for talent acquisition.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: This practice raises ethical questions since employers have access only to information that applicants choose to make public.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Many Western-European countries restrict employers' use of social media in the workplace.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: States including Arkansas, California, Colorado, Illinois, Maryland, Michigan, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Utah, Washington, and Wisconsin protect applicants and employees from surrendering usernames and passwords for social media accounts.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: A 2013 survey found that one in ten people aged 16 to 34 claimed to have been rejected for a job because of social media activity.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Social media services were reported to affect deception in resumes, increasing deception about interests and hobbies.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA
